annotation.title_clean: Ethical Asymmetry in Human-Robot Interaction – An Empirical Test of Sparrow's Hypothesis
annotation.title_en: Ethical Asymmetry in Human-Robot Interaction – An Empirical Test of Sparrow's Hypothesis
annotation.authors_or_issuer: Wang, M.; Bartneck, C.; Turp, M.-J.; Kaber, D.
annotation.venue: ACM Transactions on Human-Robot Interaction (arXiv preprint)
annotation.summary_en: Mixed within/between online experiment testing Sparrow's hypothesis that people condemn cruelty to robots more than they praise equivalent kindness. Results show a symmetrical (cubic) relationship between perceived moral permissibility and perceived virtue, so the asymmetry hypothesis is not supported. It offers behavioural evidence on human-robot moral norms, not governance.
key_provisions_or_claims: Sparrow's ethical asymmetry hypothesis was not supported.
Moral permissibility of action significantly influenced perceived permissibility and virtue scores.
Best-fit relationship between permissibility and virtue was cubic and symmetrical.
The four cardinal virtue scales behaved similarly, suggesting a global moral appraisal.
Adapted Questionnaire on Cardinal Virtues may be useful for future HRI studies.
